This is the kind of story that you (1) ____ even believe really happened – but I promise it did!
I was taking my final exams at school and we were all sitting in the big hall. It was really hot so the teacher (2) ____ to open all the windows. Usually the school kept them closed because they were very high up, which meant the teacher (3) ____ climb up a step ladder to open them.

It (5) ____ come in through the open windows.
The teacher made a speech about how we (6) ____ let it deflect our attention from our exam, and that we (7) ____ talk or anything, and then she started going around, climbing on the step ladder and trying to shoo the pigeon out of one of the windows. But the pigeon just (8) ____ find its way out at all. It was getting more and more agitated, and making more and more noise. The teacher (9) ____ expected us to just ignore it all!

sections.title: Reading: Emotions and expression
sections.instructions: Read the six-paragraph article below, then choose the best answer to each question. Base your answers on the article.

questions.prompt: The performance example in paragraph 1 is used to:
The article’s purpose is to:

sections.passage:
Must we always look happy?

1. At a school performance, a young actor waits behind the curtain. Nervousness makes his hands shake and his voice sound thin. Later, when the audience applauds, his shoulders relax and he speaks with confidence. The scene offers a familiar reminder: feelings can change how we move, sound and behave, even when we have planned exactly what to say.

2. Expressions also help people communicate without words. A friend's worried look may invite a question; an excited grin can announce good news before a conversation begins. Yet interpreting a face is not always straightforward. Someone who looks serious may simply be concentrating. It would be unfair to assume that every unsmiling person is unfriendly or unhappy.

3. Sometimes people deliberately choose an expression that does not match their mood. Imagine feeling disappointed after losing a match and then trying to smile. That action may seem counterintuitive: your expression appears to contradict what you feel. You might do it to reassure a teammate or to approach the next conversation more positively. Choosing the smile does not mean that the disappointment has disappeared.

4. People disagree about attempts to influence feelings through outward behaviour. Some welcome the idea of using a smile or a calm voice to help themselves face a difficult moment. Others feel that forcing an expression makes their experience seem less honest. Both attitudes deserve consideration. An approach that one person finds helpful may leave another feeling pressured to pretend, so a universal rule would overlook important differences.

5. The pressure can be especially noticeable at work. A receptionist may be expected to sound cheerful while dealing with an impatient customer. This management of displayed feelings is often called emotional labour. In an imagined workplace where staff must hide every trace of frustration, an employee could finish the day feeling exhausted and unheard. The difficulty is not simply being polite; it is being given no space to acknowledge difficult experiences. Managers should consider that burden when setting expectations for customer service.

6. There is a difference between choosing a helpful response and being required to wear a permanent smile. People need room to decide how to manage and express their feelings in different situations, while still treating others respectfully. A quiet moment, an honest conversation or a deliberate smile may each have a place. The aim should be a thoughtful choice, not a demand that everyone look happy all the time.

sections.title: Writing: A letter to the editor
sections.instructions: Identify the article, express your opinion, support it with at least two details in your own words, consider another view, and conclude with a suggestion. Use a formal tone and at least three hedging expressions.

questions.prompt: Write your own 200–250 word letter to the editor responding to the article.

sections.passage:
Start: Dear Editor,
Paragraph 1: article and opinion.
Paragraphs 2–3: reasons, article evidence and another viewpoint.
Paragraph 4: conclusion or suggestion.
Close: Yours faithfully, + your name.
Useful phrases: I am writing in response to…; While I recognise…; I am not entirely convinced…; Furthermore…; Nevertheless…; I would therefore argue…
Hedging: believe, suggest, appear, seem, may, might, could, would, perhaps, probably, somewhat, to some extent.
Rubric: response/opinion 2; evidence/reasons 2; organisation/format 2; vocabulary/tone/hedging 2; grammar/spelling/punctuation 2.
